name: Features-versus-neurons score histogram
summary: Two populations of units — the autoencoder's learned features and the transformer's own MLP neurons — scored on one number and drawn as overlapping histograms on a shared axis. It is how the paper argues at population scale, rather than by example, that its features are more interpretable and more reproducible than neurons.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper's claim is comparative and population-wide. Its unit of analysis, the [[feature]] — a direction in activation space recovered by a [[sparse-autoencoder]] — is offered in place of the MLP neuron, which it treats as a bad unit because one neuron responds to unrelated things ([[polysemanticity]]), plausibly because the layer carries more features than neurons ([[superposition]]). Case studies show that particular features are clean, not that features in general beat neurons — and the paper concedes its case studies are [[cherry-picked-case-studies|chosen ones]].

So every unit gets one score and both populations are drawn at once. A two-row table of means would hide the shape that matters: in the hand-scored figure the neuron mean is 3.2 but the neuron median is 0 — most neurons admitted no interpretation at all, and a thin minority scored well. A bar chart of averages would not say whether the gap is a whole population shifted or a tail doing the work. Overlaying makes separation, or its absence, the visible fact, and puts the disconfirming evidence — where the two coincide — inside the same frame.

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is one score computed once per unit, and a unit is either one autoencoder feature or one of the 512 ReLU neurons in the MLP of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer model]] ([[neuron-notation]]). Which score changes by figure: a 0–14 rubric total, a [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true activations, a yes/no accuracy, a [[pearson-correlation]] against the closest counterpart in a second model.

The vertical axis is usually Density, not Count. Each population is normalised separately to enclose area 1, because the populations are unequal — about 3,676 features against 512 neurons — and counts would hide the neurons. The price is that bar height says nothing about how many units were scored. To convert, multiply height by bin width: height $4$ over bins of width $0.02$ is about $8\%$ of that population. Only the hand-scored figure uses Count, its samples being small and similar in size.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, yellow appears where a third population does ([[randomized-transformer]]). Dark navy is the two translucent fills lying over each other — overlap, not a third group, and the trap the chart sets.

Look first at the small triangles beneath the axis: the medians. The distance between them is the claim. Then the dotted "random chance" line, if there is one, and whether the teal mode sits on it. Then the legend chips, repeating median and mean and giving a "failures" count — runs where the scoring model replied in a format the scoring code could not parse, so the unit was dropped rather than scored badly. It describes the pipeline, not the units. No claim is read off a single bar.

### What a bad result would look like

Two histograms lying on top of each other: mostly navy, one shared mode, the triangles nearly touching. That would say the learned directions are no easier to explain than the neurons the model already had — that [[dictionary-learning]] bought nothing. Weaker failures count too: crimson beating teal on the mean while both share a mode, so a tail carries the average and the typical feature is no better; or teal sitting well clear of the chance line, undercutting the premise that neurons are hard to read at all. The importance-weighted appendix figure comes close to that first picture, and the paper prints it anyway.

### Where it comes back

Fig-39 is the human arm: a [[feature-interpretability-rubric|rubric]] total from a single [[blinded-annotation|blinded]] rater, counts rather than density, medians 12 against 0. Fig-40 and fig-41 are the two [[automated-interpretability]] arms — activation prediction (0.58 against 0.2, with a tall teal spike at exactly zero that is a scoring convention, not a result) and [[automated-logit-scoring|logit-weight prediction]] against a 0.5 chance line (0.73 against 0.53). Fig-52 reuses the shape for [[universality]]: the axis becomes agreement with the closest match in a separately trained model, medians 0.72 against 0.46. Fig-71 replots fig-40's score after [[importance-scoring]] corrects the sampling, and both populations slump toward zero. Fig-72 is the odd one out: three populations in stacked rows rather than overlaid, its axis explanation length rather than a score — a caveat check whose good outcome is three rows that look alike.
